finding.claim: GET /invoice/<inv_id> has no authorization check, so any caller can read any customer's invoice by ID (IDOR). The sibling /my/invoice route performs the ownership check; this one does not.
finding.source: inv_id from the URL path (attacker-controlled); caller identity is never consulted. Precondition: no outer login gate is visible in this file, and if one exists it still allows any logged-in customer to read other customers' invoices.
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10 returns the full invoice record, including the customer field, for any ID.

trace.note: Route registered with no auth decorator.
get_invoice(inv_id) receives the attacker-supplied path parameter.
INVOICES.get(inv_id) or abort(404) looks up any record by ID; no ownership comparison.

finding.guards_checked: No ownership comparison against inv['customer'] or g.user on this route. No auth decorator. No before_request hook in this file. Contrast with /my/invoice/<inv_id> (lines 13-18), which does compare owner to caller and returns 404 otherwise, and /my/invoices (lines 21-23), which filters by owner. Unverified: any app-wide auth middleware outside this file.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only route decorator on /invoice/<inv_id> is @app.route at invoices.py:7; there is no login_required, before_request, or before_app_request anywhere in the directory (Grep found only the three @app.route lines). get_invoice at invoices.py:9-10 does a bare INVOICES.get(inv_id) or abort(404) and jsonify(inv) with no owner comparison, unlike get_my_invoice at invoices.py:16-17.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: invoices.py:7-10 has no auth decorator and no ownership check, so anyone who can reach the route can fetch any invoice by ID. The only residual uncertainty is app-wide middleware that would live outside this directory, which I could not inspect; within the available code, nothing blocks it.

finding.claim: The ownership checks in /my/invoice/<inv_id> and /my/invoices are only as sound as the code that sets g.user, which is not in this file. If g.user is populated from unverified input (e.g., a header or query parameter), both checks can be bypassed.
finding.source: Unknown: the origin of g.user is outside the provided code. Precondition: g.user is set from attacker-controllable input somewhere else in the application.
finding.sink: Ownership comparison inv['customer'] != g.user['id'] at invoices.py:16, and the filter i['customer'] == g.user['id'] at invoices.py:23, which together gate access to other customers' invoices.

trace.note: Authorization decision relies on g.user['id'] being the authenticated caller.
List filter relies on the same g.user['id'].

finding.guards_checked: Within this file: ownership comparisons are present and correct, and a missing match returns 404. Not verified: how g.user is populated, whether it is authenticated, and whether anonymous requests reach these routes (an unset g.user raises an unhandled error here, a 500 rather than a 401).

verdict.guard_found: Ownership checks within the file: invoices.py:16-17 compares inv["customer"] to g.user["id"] and aborts 404 on mismatch; invoices.py:23 filters list results by the same comparison. No other file in the directory sets g.user, so no authentication or population guard is visible.
verdict.reason: The trace lines at invoices.py:16, 17, and 23 match the candidate's description, but the claimed bypass depends on how g.user is populated, and the only file provided is invoices.py (grep for g.user or before_request finds only lines 16 and 23), so whether attacker-controlled input can set g.user cannot be decided from this code.
